tldr: To help bipedal robots with large feet walk stably on yielding terrain like sand and foam, the authors developed "MILD": a contact solver that discretizes the foot to calculate eccentric penetration accurately and quickly, paired with a reinforcement learning method that adapts in real time using latent modulation of terrain properties.
hero_caption: A bipedal robot traverses diverse deformable surfaces of varying stiffness: rubber tiles, three densities of polyurethane foam, grass, and sand. By integrating a physics-based, fast contact solver with a reinforcement learning pipeline, the robot achieves adaptive locomotion across unknown sinkage conditions.
overview:
Real-world environments where robots are needed most—such as disaster zones and planetary surfaces—are often soft and deformable, covered with sand, soil, or rubble. Yet, most bipedal locomotion controllers have been designed assuming rigid, unyielding ground. The main bottleneck is that standard robot simulators rely on rigid-body contacts, making it hard to simulate foot penetration and its complex spatiotemporal reaction forces fast enough for training.

Furthermore, unlike quadrupeds with small point feet, bipedal robots have large, flat soles. When stepping onto yielding terrain, the foot often penetrates obliquely or off-center, causing resistive forces to vary dramatically across the sole. Assuming a uniform reaction force across the entire foot, as prior work often did, deviates sharply from real sinkage behavior and easily leads to falls on hardware.

To solve this, the authors developed "MILD," a novel contact solver that discretizes the foot into 154 micro-elements. Each element computes granular resistive force and added-mass effects independently while maintaining rigid-body kinematic constraints across the whole foot. They paired this with a deep reinforcement learning framework that estimates foot velocity to modulate terrain properties in latent space, adjusting the walking gait on the fly.

In hardware tests using the 12-DoF bipedal robot "EngineAI SA01," the system walked stably without any prior terrain knowledge across surfaces ranging from stiff rubber tiles to deep-sinking, low-density polyurethane foam, as well as real grass and sand. It automatically tuned stride length and foot clearance, achieving remarkable robustness without tripping—even when crossing sharp, sudden boundaries between different stiffness levels.
contributions: Proposed a discrete-element contact solver that models eccentric penetration and heterogeneous force distributions under large bipedal feet in real time with high physical fidelity.
Integrated relative kinematic constraints across elements with friction cone limits, coupling the solver with whole-body dynamics while preventing foot penetration artifacts and unrealistic slipping.

Developed a reinforcement learning framework that estimates foot velocity from proprioception (joint angles, angular velocities, etc.) and modulates latent representations to identify and adapt to terrain stiffness online.

Demonstrated on hardware higher traversal success rates, improved energy efficiency, and immediate adaptation to unknown terrain transitions on graded foams, grass, and sand compared to existing methods.

sections.heading: Why is walking on soft ground so hard for bipedal robots?
sections.summary: Most real-world surfaces yield and deform, but standard simulators rely on rigid contact and fail to reproduce sinkage accurately. Moreover, bipedal robots have large feet where point-contact assumptions fail, requiring a new modeling approach that handles eccentric penetration.
sections.details:
Bipedal robots have huge potential in unstructured, deformable environments, but most existing locomotion controllers are optimized purely for rigid terrain. Mainstream simulators (such as MuJoCo and Isaac Gym) rely on rigid-body dynamics. They cannot capture the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of yielding ground, making it difficult to generate training data that transfers well to hardware.

For physics-based modeling of deformable substrates, particle-level granular media (GM) simulations exist, but simulating a single second can take days, ruling them out for reinforcement learning. To reduce computational cost, spring-damper models and Resistive Force Theory (RFT: an empirical model describing quasi-static reaction forces) have been proposed. However, these fail to capture inertial impact forces during high-speed foot penetration and the "added-mass effect," where jammed sand beneath the foot accelerates alongside it.

A bigger hurdle is the sheer size of a biped's foot. Prior legged locomotion studies on deformable terrain focused mostly on single-DoF hoppers or quadrupeds with point-like feet. For those, assuming a uniform force distribution across the contact patch was a workable simplification. For flat bipedal feet, however, landing angles naturally cause "eccentric penetration," where the toe or heel sinks much deeper than the rest. The resistive forces and granular flow vary drastically across different parts of the sole, causing the uniform distribution assumption to break down completely.

To bridge this sim-to-real gap, the authors propose MILD (Tractable Model achieving Improved bipedal Locomotion on Deformables), an efficient and tractable deformable terrain model designed specifically for bipedal locomotion.

sections.heading: A 154-element contact solver and latent-modulated reinforcement learning
sections.summary: The foot sole is discretized into micro-elements, each calculating its own granular jamming cone and added mass to reproduce uneven sinkage forces. On the learning side, an RL framework dynamically modulates a terrain latent embedding using estimated foot velocities.
sections.details:
The core of this approach consists of two components: a physics-grounded discrete-element contact solver and a terrain-aware reinforcement learning pipeline.

- Discrete-Element Granular Model (II-A)
The entire sole is meshed into 154 micro-elements (0.0195 m per unit). When an element penetrates the ground, it models a conical jamming zone forming directly beneath it. As penetration depth increases, the cone expands, increasing the trapped sand mass (added mass $m_A$). The normal reaction force $F_{GM}$ is calculated analytically in closed form, incorporating both static bearing capacity and momentum transfer (inertial drag) from colliding with the added mass. This allows real-time simulation of large local resistive spikes during angled landings and sharp impact forces during high-speed touchdowns.

- Whole-Body Dynamics and Rigid Kinematic Solver (II-B)
Calculating forces independently per element would cause the elements on a single rigid sole to move inconsistently. To resolve this, the authors derive velocity changes across the sole from floating-base equations of motion via Jacobians, imposing kinematic constraints that drive relative velocity errors $\bm{\delta}_{rb}$ between elements to zero. For tangential forces (friction), they developed an algorithm (Algorithm 1) that solves friction cone constraints while adding a correction term to enforce zero target velocity and rigid-body consistency. Horizontal movement also incurs a drift resistive force proportional to accumulated path length from the entry point, faithfully capturing how soft sand drags on the foot.

- Terrain-Aware Reinforcement Learning Pipeline (II-C)
The policy is trained with an asymmetric Actor-Critic setup. The Critic receives privileged ground-truth terrain states from the simulator, while the Actor on the robot takes only historical proprioceptive observations (joint positions, velocities, command velocities, etc.). The key innovations here are a multi-head VAE and a "Modulation net." The VAE estimates foot velocity $\bm{v}^f_t$, foot clearance, and base velocity while generating a latent vector $\bm{z}_t$ encoding environmental properties. Because foot rebound dynamics change on softer terrain, the estimated foot velocity is used in an affine transformation $\tilde{\bm{z}}_t = \theta_1 \cdot \bm{z}_t + \theta_2$ to dynamically adjust the latent vector to terrain stiffness. Receiving this modulated embedding, the Actor senses the degree of sinkage purely through proprioception—without cameras—and immediately adjusts its gait.

captions.F2: Overview of the proposed Discrete-Element (DE) contact model. (A) Discretizing the sole into 154 elements; (B) each element forms an individual jamming cone to compute normal force $F_{GM}$; (C) satisfying element-wise friction cone and rigid-body consistency constraints simultaneously; and (D) applying horizontal drift resistance $F_D$ based on traversed distance.
captions.F4: Overall simulation and learning pipeline. The top-level contact solver computes heterogeneous yielding forces at 1000 Hz and passes them to the learner below. The VAE estimates privileged states and the latent vector $z_t$, which is refined into $\tilde{z}_t$ by the foot-velocity modulation network and fed to the Actor to output adaptive joint commands.

sections.heading: Diverse simulation data leads to remarkable hardware adaptability
sections.summary: Trained across 4096 parallel environments in Isaac Gym, the method was evaluated on the 12-DoF bipedal robot SA01. The solver exposed the agent to a rich variety of sinkage and drift scenarios in simulation, enabling the physical robot to traverse rubber, three foam stiffnesses, grass, and sand with zero falls and seamless adaptation to sudden surface changes.
sections.details:
Experiments combined Isaac Gym simulation training (~42.4 hours on an RTX 4080) and hardware evaluations on the EngineAI SA01 bipedal robot (12 leg DoFs, 100 Hz PD control).

- Simulation Comparisons (III-B)
Compared to baseline contact models (concentric spring, concentric cone, uniform RFT, eccentric spring), the proposed model produced the deepest sinkage (+38% over the eccentric spring) and the widest spread of horizontal drift (Fig. F5). This exposed the RL agent to far more diverse and challenging contact states during training, building strong robustness against extreme real-world sinkage. Compared to passivity-based controllers known for deformable surfaces, the proposed method significantly reduced lateral center-of-mass (CoM) sway, achieving much smoother walking.

- Hardware Implicit Adaptation and Baseline Comparison (III-C)
Hardware testbeds included rubber tiles as a stiff baseline, three polyurethane (PU) foams of decreasing density and stiffness (60d, 45d, and 28d), plus outdoor grass and sand. Under the proposed controller, the robot implicitly detected sinkage and automatically increased swing-leg foot clearance to avoid dragging and tripping (Fig. F7 left). On the softest 28d foam, baselines trained on other contact models failed to lift their feet enough, hitting joint limits or falling over. In contrast, the proposed policy achieved an over 95% success rate with superior energy efficiency (Fig. F7 right).

Against state-of-the-art RL baselines—a transformer-based policy (HT-2) and a clock-signal policy (Clock)—the proposed method lowered the cost of transport (COT) and joint torques substantially while demonstrating far better command velocity tracking.

- Latent Space Structure and Online Terrain Transitions
A t-SNE visualization of the modulated latent vector $\tilde{\bm{z}}_t$ across 15 seconds of walking on each substrate showed clean clustering along the terrain stiffness gradient, placing stiff rubber on the outer rim and the softest 28d foam at the center (Fig. F8). When the robot stepped abruptly from a rubber tile onto soft PU foam, its latent state shifted in real time, widening its stride immediately to maintain dynamic stability without prior cues. The controller adapted cleanly even across sharp transitions unseen during training, confirming it captures the underlying physical properties rather than superficial motion patterns.

captions.F5: Comparison of penetration depth (horizontal axis) and horizontal drift (vertical axis) distributions across contact models. The proposed model (blue) covers the widest range in both depth and drift compared to spring and uniform RFT models, exposing the agent to more diverse, challenging contact scenarios during training.
captions.F7: Left: Foot clearance across different terrains, showing the robot automatically lifts its feet higher on softer PU foams and sand. Right: Performance comparison on deep-sinking 28D foam, where the proposed method (Ours) achieves the highest success rate and lowest energy dissipation (best efficiency).
captions.F8: 2D t-SNE visualization of the modulated latent variable $\tilde{z}_t$ across terrains of varying stiffness. The stiffest rubber tile (green) sits on the outside, while softer PU foams (blue, light blue, orange) cluster concentrically along the stiffness gradient, showing clear separation of terrain stiffness.

sections.heading: Summary and what comes next
sections.summary: MILD pairs a tractable, accurate deformable contact solver for large-footed bipeds with latent-modulated reinforcement learning. It demonstrated excellent traversal across diverse hardware surfaces, paving the way for visual integration and dynamic gaits like running and jumping.
sections.details:
This work introduced MILD, an integrated framework enabling bipedal robots to walk across diverse real-world deformable terrains. By discretizing the foot into a mesh and solving eccentric penetration, high-speed impact, and non-uniform force distributions in closed form, the contact model produces rich, physically valid training data inside the simulator. In addition, an RL policy using foot velocity to modulate latent embeddings identifies and adapts to terrain stiffness online, proving remarkably stable during continuous walking and sharp stiffness transitions on hardware.

Looking ahead, the authors plan to incorporate visual sensing from cameras to anticipate surface deformation before stepping on it. While the current study focuses on steady walking, extending the contact model to highly dynamic gaits like jumping and running, as well as integrating it into classical model-based control frameworks like Model Predictive Control (MPC), are also promising future directions.

takeaways: For bipedal robots with large feet walking on deformable terrain, modeling eccentric penetration and non-uniform force distributions across the sole is essential.
Discretizing the sole into elements, applying an analytical added-mass model, and enforcing rigid-body kinematic constraints balances simulation speed and physical fidelity for RL.
Pairing privileged learning and VAEs with a modulation network driven by foot velocity—where contact differences are most pronounced—is highly effective for blind terrain stiffness adaptation.
Upgrading the simulator contact model to broaden the range of experienced contact scenarios directly improves sim-to-real success rates and hardware adaptability.
limitations: The number of discretized sole elements (154 in this paper) was chosen heuristically; optimal scaling rules for different foot shapes and sizes remain undefined.

Without exteroceptive vision (e.g., cameras) to anticipate softness in advance, adaptation only begins after touchdown and force feedback, meaning it cannot preemptively avoid extreme sinkholes or sharp drop-offs.
Evaluation was limited to periodic steady walking (up to 1.2 m/s); the validity of the contact model under more violent impacts, such as jumping, abrupt stopping, or running, remains untested.
